newsitem.title: UK: Europe, U.S. naphtha prices to fall by 2000 - study.
newsitem.headline: Europe, U.S. naphtha prices to fall by 2000 - study.

text.p: Naphtha prices in Europe and the United States, reversing the trend of the last two years, will head lower into the year 2000 as growing North African supply outstrips moderate demand, according to a study by New York-based Poten and Partners.

By the turn of the century, however, western Europe and the Far East will need extra supply from the Middle East and the Americas to feed their growing petrochemical production, and North America "will discontinue regular imports from east of Suez," it said.
"Today's high naphtha prices do not signal a new trend," Poten, a brokerage and consulting group, said.
"In fact, a tight tightening of west Europe's naphtha supply in the mid-1990s should ease late in the decade as alternative feedstocks satisfy more of ethylene's moderate demand growth."

Northwest Europe prices of naphtha, a leading feedstock for the petrochemical industry and a fundamental ingredient for making gasoline, jumped nearly 60 percent since the middle of 1995, to $233 a tonne this month.
The rally has already cooled off, with NWE cargoes pulling back to about $203/$205, including cost, insurance and freight, on Wednesday.

Paraffinic naphtha in Northwest Europe should edge lower from $169 a tonne in 1995 to $161 in 2000 and then climb back to $169 by 2005, Poten said. Prices in the U.S. Gulf will fall from $168 in 1995 to $166 in 2000 and 2005.
Singapore trends will be the reverse, with prices tacking on $3 a tonne by 2000 to $166, and then slipping back to $161 by 2005, Poten predicted.

"As 2000 approaches, the world's largest source of merchant cargoes, the Middle East, will need to push marginal barrels beyond Suez into the Western Hemisphere to maintain market equilibrium in the Far East and Europe," Poten said.

"The East, between greatly increased local production and imports from Arabian Gulf countries, will have all the naphtha it needs," it said. "West Europe, by capturing rising North African supply, will easily cover its slowly growing merchant requirement."

In western Europe demand will remain essentially unchanged to the year 2000 at 40.4 million, 400 tonnes per annum. Local supply will drop by 300,000 tonnes a year and therefore widen the region's deficit to 8.7 million tonnes a year, from 8.5 million, Poten said.
By 2005, western Europe will need 10.1 million tonnes a year from other parts of the world, it said.

"In 2000 west Europe will draw just slightly more paraffinic naphtha from the rest of the world than it did in 1995," Poten said. "Significantly, imports from the Middle East should decline. North Africa should have more volume to offer which will displace east of Suez material."
A larger amount of naphtha will trade between countries by 2005, but it will account for nine percent less of total supply, it said.
Naphtha will also cost more relative to crude in 2005 than it did in 1995, it said.

Europe's petrochemical industry grew at a rate in the first half of the 1990s that is unlikely to be surpassed, with steam cracker capacity slowing from a 4.8 percent rate to 1.9 pct in the next few years and then a meager 0.6 after the turn of the century, Poten said.
Western Europe's ethylene plants produce about 60 percent of their ethylene from naphtha, a market share likely to be frozen until 2005, Poten said.

Germany, the largest buyer of naphtha for making ethylene in Europe, will boost its demand by 30 percent from 1995 to 2005 and "will almost single-handedly increase west Europe's demand for ethylene feed naphtha" in that period, Poten said.
